strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians from arbitrary unposed and uncalibrated multi-view inputs (spanning from sparse 2-view to dense 32-view settings).

Well-motivated pipeline design: the proposed 3D-annotation-free training leverages geometry foundation models (VGGT) for geometric pseudo-labels and view coverage mask filtering for novel-view photometric supervision, enabling training on large-scale multi-view datasets (InstanceMV-14K).

Effective technical components: the instance-guided contrastive loss substantially reduces the complexity from traditional pixel-wise contrastive learning $O(N_p^2)$ to $O(N_p K)$ while sharpening instance boundaries; the geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification intuitively exploits the spatial sparsity of high-level semantics to save memory and compute.

Strong empirical performance: quantitatively and qualitatively outperforms recent feed-forward baselines (LSM, Uni3R) across varying view counts (2 to 32 views) on ScanNet, and demonstrates a massive speedup (seconds vs. 10-15+ minutes) over per-scene optimization methods (LangSplat, LangScene-X) while achieving superior mIoU and mAcc.
weaknesses: Clarity/typographical issue in the sparsification formulation: on page 6, the text states that $S_{sem}$ semantic Gaussians are obtained 'using a smaller voxel size $\epsilon_{sem}$' to achieve higher sparsity than geometry Gaussians ($S_{sem} < S_{geo}$). A smaller voxel edge length typically creates finer voxels and thus a larger number of voxels, whereas a larger voxel size $\epsilon_{sem}$ would yield coarser, fewer voxels. This needs clarification.

Unsubstantiated claims regarding 3D editing: While the title, abstract, and Figure 1 advertise 3D editing as a key capability enabled by FLEG, there are no experimental results, detailed methodology, or qualitative visualizations demonstrating 3D editing in Section 4.

Heavy reliance on upstream foundation models: The model architecture, depth/pose distillation, and coverage masks are fundamentally anchored in VGGT. The paper lacks analysis on failure modes or sensitivity when the upstream VGGT predictions contain severe depth or pose errors.

Limited evaluation domain and missing computational resource details: Experiments are conducted exclusively on indoor scan datasets (ScanNet / ScanNet++). Furthermore, given that the model contains ~1B parameters and trains on a dataset of 15 million images, details regarding training hardware, batch sizes, and GPU hours are missing.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: reconstructing language-embedded 3D Gaussian representations in a single feed-forward pass from uncalibrated and unposed multi-view inputs, handling both sparse and dense view regimes.

The geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification strategy is technically well-motivated, leveraging the spatial sparsity and lower directional variation of semantic features relative to continuous geometry and appearance.

The 3D-annotation-free training scheme and instance-guided contrastive loss effectively reduce computational complexity from $O(N_p^2)$ to $O(N_p K)$ while enhancing feature boundary sharpness and multi-view semantic consistency.

Significant inference speedup over per-scene optimization methods (seconds vs. 10–20 minutes) while demonstrating superior segmentation performance against existing sparse-view feed-forward baselines (e.g., LSM, Uni3R).
weaknesses: Heavy dependence on pretrained foundation models: The pipeline relies substantially on VGGT for camera pose estimation, depth/point-map supervision, and target view selection. Any systematic artifacts, scale drift, or failures of VGGT on challenging scenes directly impact training, yet there is little analysis of the model's robustness or sensitivity to pseudo-ground-truth noise.

Selective comparison in Table 2: When comparing against per-scene optimization methods (LangSplat, LangScene-X), the paper only reports segmentation metrics (mIoU, mAcc) and runtime, omitting novel-view synthesis metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Per-scene 3DGS typically achieves significantly higher photorealism on dense views; omitting these metrics hides the appearance quality trade-offs inherent to feed-forward estimation.

Evaluation scope is limited mainly to indoor room-scale datasets (ScanNet and ScanNet++). Given the claims of general applicability from 'any views' and video data, validation on outdoor or object-centric benchmarks would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

The ablation studies in Table 3 are relatively coarse: crucial design decisions—such as the 3D feature aggregation module, the isotropic approximation versus anisotropic semantic Gaussians, and sensitivity to the semantic voxel size $\epsilon_{sem}$—are not systematically isolated or ablated.

Claims regarding downstream utility (e.g., 3D editing and robotic interaction highlighted in the Introduction and Figure 1) are primarily supported by qualitative snapshots rather than rigorous quantitative evaluation or user studies.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: lifting arbitrary numbers of uncalibrated, unposed multi-view images directly into language-embedded 3D Gaussian Splatting in a single feed-forward pass.

The geometry–semantic hierarchical sparsification strategy is well-motivated by the observation that high-level semantics exhibit lower spatial frequency than geometry/appearance; decoupling and aggregating semantic Gaussians via isotropic moment-matching reduces Gaussian memory footprint from 6.4M to 2.6M while maintaining accuracy.

The 3D-annotation-free training pipeline effectively leverages 2D foundation models (VGGT, SAM2, CLIP) and incorporates a coverage-mask-based novel view selection mechanism for cross-view photometric supervision.

The instance-guided contrastive learning loss reduces the complexity of pixel-wise contrastive learning from O(N_p^2) to O(N_p K) while significantly improving semantic boundary discrimination (mIoU improves from 39.01 to 44.58 on ScanNet++).

Consistently outperforms existing feed-forward baselines across sparse (2-view) to dense (32-view) settings, and achieves orders of magnitude faster inference compared to per-scene optimization approaches (e.g., LangSplat) with superior segmentation accuracy.
weaknesses: Reliance and error propagation from pretrained models: The framework heavily relies on pseudo-labels (poses, depths) predicted by VGGT and 2D masks from SAM2. The manuscript does not discuss how robust the system is when VGGT makes inaccurate camera pose or depth predictions, particularly in textureless or geometrically ambiguous scenes.

Ablations could be more comprehensive: Key components such as the multi-view 3D feature aggregation module, the coverage threshold tau for novel view selection, and the isotropic vs. anisotropic semantic covariance formulation in Eq. (12) lack dedicated ablation experiments.

Limited evaluation domains: Quantitative experiments are confined to indoor datasets (ScanNet and ScanNet++). Given that training incorporates RealEstate10K, evaluating generalization on outdoor or diverse in-the-wild datasets would make the empirical validation stronger.

Downstream tasks claimed in Figure 1 (such as 3D editing and robotic query) are mentioned in the introduction and teaser figure but lack detailed quantitative analysis or comprehensive qualitative demonstrations in the main text.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge: feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians from arbitrary, uncalibrated, and unposed multi-view images without requiring ground-truth 3D geometry or semantic annotations.

A well-motivated and insightful decoupling strategy (DGLE): recognizing that semantic fields have much lower spatial complexity than geometry and appearance, the proposed decoupled semantic Gaussians achieve comparable semantic fidelity using less than 5% of the embeddings, drastically saving storage and rendering memory.

The dual-branch distillation framework is technically sound: novel-view distillation effectively mitigates overfitting to input views while maintaining pose-free stability, and the instance-guided contrastive learning effectively improves cross-instance boundary discriminability with linear O(NpK) complexity.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across diverse input view configurations (2 to 16 views, plus dense 32 views) on ScanNet and ScanNet++, as well as zero-shot generalization on Replica, showing clear superiority over existing feed-forward and per-scene optimization baselines.
weaknesses: Several downstream capabilities claimed in the abstract and introduction (such as 3D editing) are barely demonstrated or analyzed in the main text; the empirical validation focuses almost entirely on novel view synthesis and open-vocabulary 2D query segmentation.

The evaluation of 3D open-vocabulary capability is conducted entirely via 2D rendered feature maps (mIoU / mAcc from novel views). Evaluating on explicit 3D semantic segmentation metrics (e.g., 3D mIoU on point clouds) would provide a stronger verification of the spatial consistency of the decoupled semantic Gaussians.

The comparison against multi-view baselines (LSM and Uni3R) is slightly restricted because official weights for those models only accept two views, necessitating a two-view selection heuristic at inference; while understandable, the comparison in multi-view regimes is therefore against truncated models.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical limitation in generalizable 3D scene representation: enabling feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians from an arbitrary number of unposed/uncalibrated input views.

The observation that semantic representations require significantly less spatial density than geometric/appearance representations is well-motivated. The Decoupled Gaussian Language Embedding (DGLE) module effectively compresses the semantic representation into a sparse set of isotropic semantic Gaussians, cutting storage overhead from ~490 MB down to ~18 MB (<5% of embeddings) while preserving segmentation accuracy.

The training pipeline is fully self-supervised with respect to 3D/semantic ground truth: it leverages VGGT for geometric distillation, novel-view selection based on point-cloud coverage to prevent overfitting, and an instance-guided contrastive loss with SAM2 and CLIP features for semantic distillation.

Extensive experimental validation across ScanNet, ScanNet++, and cross-dataset evaluation on Replica, accompanied by meaningful ablations on semantic voxel scale, contrastive learning, and novel-view distillation.
weaknesses: Overclaimed contributions regarding multi-task capabilities: The abstract, introduction, and Section 3 repeatedly mention 3D editing as a core capability supported by the representation (even featuring it in Figure 1). However, there is no experimental setup, quantitative evaluation, or qualitative result demonstrating 3D editing in either the main paper or the appendix.

Unfair/uneven baseline comparisons in multi-view settings: Feed-forward semantic baselines such as LSM and Uni3R are inherently 2-view architectures. Feeding them only the two nearest views when evaluating on 4, 8, and 16 views naturally puts them at a structural disadvantage compared to FLEG, which processes all views simultaneously. While this highlights FLEG's architectural flexibility, it somewhat conflates multi-view aggregation advantages with the quality of the semantic representation itself.

High architectural dependence on existing foundation models: The core framework heavily integrates existing systems—VGGT for pose, depth, and backbone initialization; AnySplat-style voxelization; SAM2 for masks; and CLIP for embeddings. While the engineering synthesis is effective, the fundamental methodological innovation is relatively incremental.

Clarity on semantic rendering and querying: While Section 3.3 explains the moment-matching derivation of the sparse semantic Gaussians, the rasterization/rendering procedure during inference and how depth/opacity sorting between geometric and semantic Gaussians is handled (or if semantic Gaussians are rendered completely independently) lacks sufficient formal specification.

strengths: Practical and timely problem setting: Extending feed-forward Gaussian Splatting to support language-embedded representations from arbitrary numbers of unposed and uncalibrated multi-view images addresses critical efficiency and flexibility bottlenecks in open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding.

Decoupled Gaussian Language Embedding (DGLE): Leveraging the natural sparsity difference between geometric details and high-level semantics to decouple dense geometric Gaussians from sparse, isotropic semantic Gaussians is conceptually sound and significantly reduces storage overhead (<5% embeddings of dense baselines) with negligible loss in semantic accuracy.

Effective dual-branch distillation framework: Formulating novel-view distillation with visibility-coverage-based view selection successfully prevents overfitting to context views in a pose-free regime, while instance-guided contrastive learning improves cross-instance semantic boundaries.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors validate their method across varying view counts (2 to 32 views) on ScanNet and ScanNet++, cross-dataset transfer on Replica, and auxiliary tasks including camera pose and depth estimation, demonstrating consistent performance gains over competing methods.
weaknesses: Baseline comparison constraints for multi-view settings: For feed-forward semantic baselines like LSM and Uni3R, the evaluation relies on running two-view pretrained models on the two nearest views to the target. While understandable given official checkpoints, this setup means the multi-view semantic baselines are evaluated under restricted context.

Under-explored downstream capabilities: The abstract and introduction highlight multi-task capabilities, specifically mentioning 3D editing alongside novel view synthesis and open-vocabulary object queries, but the experimental evaluation exclusively focuses on novel view synthesis and semantic segmentation/query without quantitative or detailed qualitative evaluation of 3D editing.

Evaluation limited to 2D projections: Semantic understanding is evaluated via 2D rendered feature maps (mIoU and mAcc on novel views). Evaluating 3D point/voxel semantic segmentation directly on the 3D Gaussian field would provide stronger evidence of 3D semantic consistency.

Reliance on multi-stage pseudo-supervision pipeline: The training pipeline is heavily reliant on multiple large foundation models (VGGT, SAM2, CLIP). While effective, failure modes and noise propagation from imperfect 2D masks or CLIP features under occlusion/extreme viewpoint variations are not thoroughly analyzed.
